text: Inside every large language model there are billions of numbers, and most of them belong to one small, repeated part called a neuron. The name comes from biology, but the artificial version is far simpler than a brain cell: it is a few lines of arithmetic you could do on paper. If we understand exactly what one neuron computes, the rest of a network becomes a matter of putting many of them together. So what does a single neuron actually do?

A neuron receives a list of numbers as its input, which is simply a vector, and it holds a second list of the same length called its weights. Think of the weights as the volume knobs on a mixing desk: each one decides how loudly its input is heard, and a negative weight turns that input into an argument against. The neuron multiplies each input by its weight and adds up the results, and you already know this by another name, because it is the dot product of the weight vector with the input vector.

To that sum the neuron adds one more number, called the bias. The bias does not depend on the input at all. It works like the height of a bar that the weighted sum has to clear, setting how easily the neuron is persuaded before any evidence arrives. A large positive bias makes the neuron eager to respond, while a large negative one makes it reluctant, and together the weights and the bias produce a single number that we call z.

There is a picture hiding in this formula. If the input has two entries, every input is a point on the plane, and the points where z is exactly zero form a straight line. On one side of that line z is positive, and on the other side it is negative, so the neuron is really asking which side of its line a point falls on. The weight vector points across the line toward the positive side, and changing the bias slides the line without turning it.

If the neuron stopped there, it would be a linear function, and as we will see in a later lesson, stacking linear functions never gives you anything more than another linear function. So the neuron finishes by bending its output with a fixed function called the activation. The most common one today is the rectified linear unit, or ReLU, which acts like a hinge: it passes positive values through unchanged and replaces every negative value with zero. Older networks used the sigmoid instead, a smooth curve that squeezes any number into the range between zero and one, rather like a dimmer switch that never goes fully off or fully on.

Put together, a neuron takes a weighted sum, shifts it by a bias, and bends the result. In a language model, the feed-forward part of every transformer block contains thousands of these neurons side by side, each reading the same token vector with its own weights and each bending its own sum, so the multiplications and additions you have just seen run billions of times for every token the model produces.

So a neuron is a weighted sum plus a bend, and on its own it can only divide its inputs with a single straight line. In the next lesson we place many neurons side by side to form a layer, and that one line becomes something much more flexible.
